what: The pati-paśu-pāśa vocabulary, the five brahma-mantras, ash observances and the framework of an older Śaiva ascetic path that the Mantramārga describes and outranks.

evidence.detail: paśu, pati, pāśa and the five brahma-mantras in both
the Mantramārga scriptures themselves describe the Atimārga as an earlier/lower stream
A. Sanderson's account of the Atimārga as antecedent of the Mantramārga

what: Temples and monasteries in Karnataka (and possibly members) passing from Kālāmukha to Vīraśaiva hands.

evidence.detail: D. N. Lorenzen (1972) and others: several former Kālāmukha centres (including Śrīśaila) later appear as Vīraśaiva seats, and the Kālāmukhas vanish from records as the Vīraśaivas rise; some ascetics may have joined the new movement.

The Vīraśaiva tradition does not derive itself from the Kālāmukhas: the Pañcācārya account has five ācāryas (Reṇuka and others) emerge from liṅgas in each age and teach from the Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi); the Liṅgāyata account centres on Basava and the śaraṇas at Kalyāṇa.
Caution: continuity of buildings is not continuity of doctrine; the vacana movement rejected the temple ritual that Kālāmukha priests served.

notes: Both accounts recorded; not reconciled. Specific inscriptional evidence for each transferred site was not checked in this run.

what: Skull-bowl, skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), six bone ornaments, cremation-ground setting and the figure of the skull-bearing ascetic in the Buddhist Yoginī tantras.

evidence.detail: Yāmuna's six Kāpāla insignia (ear-ornament/necklace, rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash, sacred thread) resemble the six 'seals' worn by Heruka and yogins in the Yoginī tantras (e.g. Hevajra).
Buddhist myth: Heruka subdues Maheśvara/Bhairava and his retinue and takes over their attire and sacred sites (Cakrasaṃvara cycle).
A. Sanderson argues the Yoginī tantras drew on Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha scriptures of Kāpālika character rather than directly on the Atimārga.

what: Personal affiliation of Naiyāyikas with the Pāśupatas and a shared account of the means of knowledge.

evidence.detail: Kauṇḍinya's inference as 'as before', 'from the remainder' and 'seen in general' uses the Nyāya Sūtra's terms (NS 1.1.5).
Uddyotakara is styled 'Pāśupatācārya'; Bhāsarvajña wrote both the Nyāyasāra and the Ratnaṭīkā; Jain doxographers call Naiyāyikas Śaivas and Vaiśeṣikas Pāśupatas.

what: The ash vow called pāśupata and a verbal parallel: 'having cut the root of the net of causes ... with the intellect ... fixed on Rudra'.

evidence.detail: Atharvaśiras 5 '... hitvā hetujālasya mūlam | buddhyā sañcitaṃ sthāpayitvā tu rudre' ~ PS 5.35-38 'chittvā doṣāṇāṃ hetujālasya mūlam | buddhyā | sañcittam | sthāpayitvā ca rudre'.

notes: Which text borrowed from which is not settled.

what: The five brahma-mantras (Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna) that close the adhyāyas of the Pāśupata Sūtra.

evidence.detail: The same five mantras stand in Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10 (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad).

what: The penance for killing a brahmin - living with the skull of the slain, begging and proclaiming one's deed - as model of the Kāpālika great vow, mediated by the myth of Bhairava.

evidence.detail: The Kūrma Purāṇa tells of the Lord's skull-bearing penance for brahmin-murder and its release at the tīrtha.
Lorenzen and others derive the mahāvrata from the Dharmaśāstra brahmahatyā penance (Manu and Yājñavalkya; verse numbers not checked here).
